gloss_terse: with one's own hand; performing an action personally, directly by oneself
gloss_readable: This Greek adjective emphasizes direct personal involvement in an action, literally 'self-handed.' In its single New Testament appearance, it describes the crew throwing cargo overboard with their own hands during Paul's shipwreck voyage. The term conveys the urgency and necessity of manual labor performed without delegation—when the situation is so dire that everyone must pitch in personally. Classical usage ranges from murder done by one's own hand to creative work executed personally.

senses.1: The multilingual evidence (Spanish 'con propias manos,' English 'with their own hands') confirms the concrete physical sense of personal manual action. At Acts 27:19, the ship's crew personally jettisons the tackle during the storm—an all-hands-on-deck moment where rank and role dissolve into shared survival labor.

gloss_terse: dry, dark, parched; squalid or dim due to lack of moisture or light
gloss_readable: This adjective describes dryness and dimness, often applied to parched landscapes or rough, squalid conditions. Peter uses it metaphorically for prophecy as a lamp shining 'in a dark place' until the day dawns (2 Pet 1:19). The word evokes the murky, shadowy quality of a dry, unilluminated space—whether physical drought or moral gloom. Classical Greek uses it for dry climates, rough terrain, and even disheveled hair. The New Testament appropriates this atmospheric term for spiritual illumination breaking into darkness.

senses.1: The translation spectrum (English/German 'dark,' Spanish 'oscuro,' French retaining the Greek) points to the metaphorical sense of a dim, shadowy place. Peter's 'dark place' is the world awaiting Messiah's full revelation—prophecy gives light in this interim darkness until the morning star rises in believers' hearts.

gloss_terse: unseen, hidden, invisible; not manifest or evident to sight
gloss_readable: This adjective means 'unseen' or 'hidden,' often referring to things below the earth or concealed from view. In Hebrews 4:13, it appears in the striking declaration that 'no creature is hidden from God's sight'—nothing is invisible (ἀφανής) before the One to whom we must give account. The term underscores divine omniscience: what remains unseen to human eyes is fully exposed to God. Classical usage includes references to the underworld, disappeared persons, and secret actions. The writer to the Hebrews deploys it to demolish any illusion of privacy before the all-seeing Creator.

senses.1: The translations (English 'hidden,' Spanish 'oculta,' French 'invisible,' German 'unsichtbar') cluster around concealment and invisibility. Hebrews 4:13 asserts that nothing is ἀφανής before God—no creature can hide, no thought can be concealed from the Judge who sees into the depths of the heart and pierces to the division of soul and spirit.

gloss_terse: disappearance, destruction, vanishing; the act of making invisible or causing to cease
gloss_readable: This noun denotes disappearance or destruction, the process of something vanishing from sight or existence. In Hebrews 8:13, it describes the old covenant as 'becoming obsolete and growing old' and thus 'ready to disappear' (ἀφανισμός). The term captures the twilight moment when something ancient fades into irrelevance and dissolution. Classical uses include extermination and astronomical occultation—stars eclipsed by the sun. The author of Hebrews employs it to signal the imminent obsolescence of the Mosaic economy, already aging and nearing its vanishing point with the arrival of the new covenant.

senses.1: The evidence (English/German 'disappearance,' French/German 'Verschwinden,' Spanish 'de desaparición') uniformly points to vanishing or ceasing to exist. Hebrews 8:13 uses ἀφανισμός to describe the old covenant's eschatological fade-out: it is 'ready for disappearance' because Christ has inaugurated the new and better covenant prophesied by Jeremiah.

gloss_terse: invisible, disappeared, vanished from sight; suddenly absent or hidden
gloss_readable: This adjective means 'made invisible' or 'disappeared,' describing what has vanished from view. Luke uses it at the Emmaus supper when Jesus 'became invisible' (ἄφαντος ἐγένετο) to the two disciples after breaking bread. Their eyes were opened to recognize Him, and in that instant He vanished—a sudden, supernatural withdrawal from sight. Classical usage includes soldiers missing after battle and heroes disappearing into legend. Luke's deployment is theologically loaded: the risen Christ is no mere revenant but Lord of matter and visibility, appearing and disappearing at will.

senses.1: The translations (English/Spanish 'invisible,' French 'disparu,' German retaining the Greek) reflect sudden disappearance. At Luke 24:31, Jesus becomes ἄφαντος after the disciples' eyes were opened—He vanishes the moment recognition dawns, leaving them alone with burning hearts and the imperative to testify to the resurrection.

gloss_terse: unsparing treatment, harshness, severity; lack of mercy or leniency
gloss_readable: This rare noun can mean either 'generosity' or, in New Testament usage, 'harsh treatment' or 'severity.' Paul uses it in Colossians 2:23 to critique ascetic practices that have 'an appearance of wisdom' but involve 'harsh treatment of the body' (ἀφειδία σώματος). The term captures the self-inflicted rigor of those who punish the flesh in pursuit of spiritual merit. Paradoxically, such unsparing severity toward the body is 'of no value against fleshly indulgence'—it cannot curb the appetites it seeks to mortify. Paul exposes the futility of self-imposed austerity divorced from Christ.

senses.1: The evidence (English 'harsh treatment,' Spanish 'severidad,' German 'Strenge') points to severity or rigor. Colossians 2:23 critiques human regulations that demand bodily ἀφειδία—unsparing ascetic discipline—as if physical deprivation could produce spiritual transformation. Paul insists that true transformation comes not from self-punishment but from union with the crucified and risen Christ.

gloss_terse: simplicity, sincerity, unworldliness; straightforward innocence without guile
gloss_readable: This noun denotes simplicity or sincerity, a straightforward, uncomplicated disposition free from duplicity. Luke describes the early believers in Acts 2:46 as eating together 'with gladness and simplicity of heart' (ἀφελότητι καρδίας). The term evokes a childlike directness and communal authenticity—no social pretense, no calculated networking, just genuine fellowship. Classical usage emphasizes unworldliness and lack of sophistication. Luke paints an idealized portrait of the Jerusalem church's common life, marked by joy and ἀφελότης—a pure, transparent togetherness rooted in shared devotion to Christ.

senses.1: The translations (English 'simplicity,' Spanish 'sencillez,' French 'simplicité') uniformly emphasize sincerity and straightforwardness. Acts 2:46 portrays the early community's table fellowship as characterized by ἀφελότης—an unadorned, heartfelt sharing that embodies the gospel's power to dissolve social barriers and create genuine koinonia.

gloss_terse: to arrive at, reach, come to; to attain or extend to a destination
gloss_readable: This verb means 'to arrive at' or 'reach,' describing the completion of a journey or the attainment of a goal. Paul uses it in Romans 16:19 when he says 'your obedience has reached everyone' (ἀφίκετο εἰς πάντας)—their faithful witness has become widely known. The term conveys the idea of reputation or influence spreading to a destination. Classical Greek uses it extensively for physical arrival, but Paul employs it metaphorically for the propagation of fame or report. The Roman believers' obedience has traveled far, becoming a matter of public knowledge and apostolic rejoicing.

senses.1: The evidence (English 'has reached,' Spanish 'ha llegado,' French 'parvenir,' German 'ankommen') confirms the sense of arrival or attainment. Romans 16:19 uses ἀφικνέομαι to describe how the report of the Romans' obedience has reached (arrived at) all people—their faithfulness has become internationally known, spreading as far as Paul's missionary circuits extend.

gloss_terse: not loving good, hostile to virtue; opposed to what is noble or beneficial
gloss_readable: This rare compound adjective means 'not loving the good' or 'hostile to virtue.' Paul includes it in his grim catalog of last-days characteristics in 2 Timothy 3:3: people will be 'not loving good' (ἀφιλάγαθοι), along with being lovers of self, lovers of money, and lovers of pleasure. The term denotes an active aversion to virtue—not mere neutrality but antagonism toward the noble and beneficial. It describes those whose affections are so disordered that they despise goodness itself. Paul warns Timothy that such moral inversion will mark the final age.

senses.1: The translations (English 'not loving good,' Spanish 'sin amor al bien,' German 'nicht das Gute liebend') all capture the compound's negative force: ἀ-φιλάγαθοι are opposed to goodness. In 2 Timothy 3:3, this vice sits in a list of vices characterizing the 'terrible times' to come—an era when love of self eclipses love of the good, and evil becomes the preferred object of affection.

gloss_terse: arrival, coming, departure; the act of reaching or leaving a place
gloss_readable: This noun denotes arrival or, paradoxically, departure—the act of coming to or leaving a place. Paul uses it in Acts 20:29 when he warns the Ephesian elders that 'after my departure' (μετὰ τὴν ἄφιξίν μου) savage wolves will enter the flock. The term can mean either 'arrival' or 'departure' depending on context; here it clearly means Paul's leaving. Classical usage favors 'arrival,' but later Greek extends it to departure. Paul's warning is sobering: his protective presence will soon be removed, and false teachers will infiltrate. The ἄφιξις marks a transition from apostolic oversight to congregational vigilance.

senses.1: The evidence (English/French 'departure,' Spanish 'partida') confirms the sense of leaving. Acts 20:29 uses ἄφιξις to mark the moment of Paul's departure from Ephesus—after he leaves, wolves will come. The term captures the vulnerability of the flock once the shepherd-apostle is gone, heightening the urgency of the elders' responsibility to guard the church.

gloss_terse: to make like, liken, compare; to render similar or assimilate
gloss_readable: This verb means 'to make like' or 'assimilate,' describing the process of rendering one thing similar to another. In Hebrews 7:3, Melchizedek is described as 'made like the Son of God' (ἀφωμοιωμένος)—not that he is the Son, but that his scriptural portrayal (without genealogy, beginning, or end) prefigures Christ's eternal priesthood. The term emphasizes typological correspondence: Melchizedek's mysterious presentation in Genesis serves as a deliberate likeness to the timeless Son. Classical usage includes comparing or portraying in art. The author of Hebrews deploys it to underscore the divinely orchestrated resemblance between the ancient priest-king and Jesus.

senses.1: The translations (English 'made like,' Spanish 'hecho semejante,' French/German 'vergleichen' for 'compare') reflect the idea of resemblance or comparison. Hebrews 7:3 uses ἀφομοιόω to say Melchizedek has been 'made like' (depicted as resembling) the Son of God—a typological foreshadowing where the silence of Scripture about Melchizedek's origins becomes theologically eloquent, pointing to Christ's eternal priesthood.

gloss_terse: foam, froth, slaver; the foamy substance produced by agitation or disease
gloss_readable: This noun denotes foam or froth, whether from sea waves, a river, or a diseased body. Luke uses it in his account of the demon-possessed boy (Luke 9:39) who is seized by a spirit that throws him into convulsions 'with foaming' (μετὰ ἀφροῦ). The term vividly captures the physical symptoms of violent spiritual oppression—the boy's mouth froths as the unclean spirit ravages him. Classical Greek uses ἀφρός for sea foam (famously, Aphrodite born from it) and the foaming mouths of rabid animals or epileptics. Luke's clinical description underscores the brutal reality of demonic affliction, which Jesus' word instantly dispels.

senses.1: The evidence (English 'foaming,' Spanish 'espuma,' French 'écume') confirms the physical phenomenon of froth. Luke 9:39 uses ἀφροῦ to describe the boy's foaming at the mouth during demonic seizures—a graphic medical detail that heightens the pathos of the father's plea and the power of Jesus' exorcistic command.

gloss_terse: to fall asleep, doze off; to drift into sleep, especially unwittingly
gloss_readable: This verb means 'to fall asleep,' particularly in the sense of dozing off unintentionally. Luke uses it in the account of Jesus calming the storm: 'as they sailed, He fell asleep' (ἀφύπνωσεν, Luke 8:23). The term emphasizes the naturalness of Jesus' sleep—exhausted from ministry, He drifts off in the boat, fully human in His need for rest. Classical usage includes both falling asleep and waking from sleep, but the New Testament sense is clearly 'dozed off.' The detail is theologically rich: Jesus sleeps through the storm, at peace even as the disciples panic, manifesting both His humanity and His sovereign calm.

senses.1: The translations (English 'fell asleep,' Spanish 'se durmió,' French 's'endormir') uniformly indicate the act of falling asleep. Luke 8:23 uses ἀφυπνόω to depict Jesus' human weariness and restful trust—He falls asleep in the boat, oblivious to the wind and waves that terrorize His disciples, embodying the peace He will soon command the storm to adopt.

gloss_terse: Achaicus, a personal name; a man from Achaia or bearing an Achaian connection
gloss_readable: This proper noun designates Achaicus, a Christian mentioned by Paul in 1 Corinthians 16:17 alongside Stephanas and Fortunatus. These three men came from Corinth to visit Paul, supplying what was lacking and refreshing his spirit. The name likely indicates either origin from Achaia (the Roman province including Corinth) or servile status (slaves were often named after their place of origin). Paul's gratitude for Achaicus and his companions underscores the importance of face-to-face fellowship and the encouragement of loyal co-laborers who bridge distances to strengthen apostolic bonds.

senses.1: The multilingual evidence simply transliterates the name (Achaikos, Achaïcus, Achaikus), confirming it as a personal identifier. At 1 Corinthians 16:17, Achaicus is one of the Corinthian delegates who refreshed Paul's spirit by their presence—a living reminder of the church's affection and a source of apostolic joy in the midst of missionary hardship.

gloss_terse: to make useless, render worthless; to corrupt or cause to become unprofitable
gloss_readable: This verb means 'to render useless' or 'make worthless,' describing the process by which something becomes unprofitable or corrupted. Paul uses it in Romans 3:12, quoting Psalm 14: 'All have turned away, they have together become worthless' (ἠχρειώθησαν). The term captures humanity's universal moral failure—we have not merely made mistakes but have become fundamentally useless for the purpose God intended. Classical usage includes damaging or disabling. Paul's indictment is total: apart from grace, every person is ἠχρειωμένος, rendered worthless by sin's corrosive power.

senses.1: The translations (English 'became worthless,' Spanish 'se hicieron inútiles,' French 'rendre inutile,' German 'unnütz werden') all emphasize the outcome of becoming useless. Romans 3:12 uses ἀχρειόω in the passive to describe humanity's collective moral bankruptcy: 'they became worthless'—a devastating summary of the human condition before God's justifying grace.

gloss_terse: useless, unprofitable, worthless; providing no benefit or utility
gloss_readable: This adjective means 'useless' or 'unprofitable,' describing what yields no benefit. Paul employs it with a twist in his letter to Philemon regarding the runaway slave Onesimus: 'Formerly he was useless (ἄχρηστος) to you, but now he is useful (εὔχρηστος) to both you and me' (Phlm 11). Paul puns on the name Onesimus ('useful') to underscore the transformation grace has wrought: what was worthless has become valuable through conversion. Classical usage ranges from 'ineffective' to 'unkind.' Paul's wordplay captures the gospel's power to redeem and repurpose, turning the useless into the indispensable.

senses.1: The evidence (English 'useless,' Spanish 'inútil,' German 'unnütz') confirms the sense of unprofitability. Philemon 11 uses ἄχρηστος in a before-and-after contrast: Onesimus was once ἄχρηστος (useless) to Philemon, but in Christ he has become εὔχρηστος (useful)—a transformed man whose new identity eclipses his former worthlessness.

gloss_terse: truthful, not lying, without deceit; incapable of falsehood
gloss_readable: This adjective means 'truthful' or 'incapable of lying,' often applied to deities or oracles in classical Greek. Paul uses it of God in Titus 1:2: 'God, who does not lie (ἀψευδής), promised eternal life before the ages began.' The term underscores divine reliability—God's word is utterly trustworthy because His nature precludes deception. Classical usage frequently describes oracles and seers as ἀψευδής, but Paul applies it exclusively to Yahweh, whose promises are guaranteed by His unchanging character. In a world of false claims and broken promises, the ἀψευδής God is the anchor of Christian hope.

senses.1: The translations (English 'unlying,' Spanish 'no mentiroso,' German 'wahrhaftig') emphasize truthfulness and absence of deceit. Titus 1:2 attributes ἀψευδής to God—He is incapable of lying, and therefore His promise of eternal life is absolutely certain. This divine attribute grounds Paul's apostolic confidence and the believer's eschatological hope.

gloss_terse: lifeless, inanimate, without soul; lacking life or animation
gloss_readable: This adjective means 'lifeless' or 'inanimate,' describing objects without a soul or vital principle. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 14:7 to contrast musical instruments ('lifeless things,' ἄψυχα) with human speech: even flutes and harps must produce distinct notes to communicate melody, so how much more must tongues-speakers articulate intelligibly! The term emphasizes the paradox that even non-living instruments follow communicative principles—they must be 'interpreted' to be understood. Classical usage includes non-animal food and spiritless persons. Paul's argument is a fortiori: if ἄψυχα instruments require clarity, how much more must Spirit-filled speakers pursue intelligibility in worship.

senses.1: The evidence (English 'lifeless things,' Spanish 'sin vida,' French 'sans vie,' German 'leblos') uniformly denotes inanimate objects. 1 Corinthians 14:7 uses ἄψυχα of musical instruments that, despite being lifeless, still convey meaning through distinct sounds—an analogy Paul deploys to urge the Corinthians to prioritize intelligibility over ecstatic utterance in corporate worship.

gloss_terse: Baal, the Canaanite deity; the storm and fertility god opposed by Israel's prophets
gloss_readable: This proper noun designates Baal, the Canaanite storm and fertility deity whose worship repeatedly seduced Israel into idolatry. Paul alludes to the Elijah narrative in Romans 11:4, quoting God's assurance to the prophet: 'I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.' The name evokes Israel's chronic apostasy and Yahweh's preservation of a faithful remnant. In classical Hebrew, 'Baal' means 'lord' or 'master,' but it became synonymous with false worship. Paul uses the Baal story to illustrate God's ongoing election of a remnant within Israel—a pattern that continues in the gospel age.

senses.1: The evidence simply transliterates the name (Baal, Baál) across languages, confirming it as the well-known Canaanite deity. Romans 11:4 invokes Baal to recall Elijah's despair and God's reassurance of a hidden remnant—a typological precedent for Paul's argument that God has not rejected Israel but continues to preserve a believing minority by grace.

gloss_terse: step, degree, standing; a position or rank attained, often metaphorically
gloss_readable: This noun originally means 'step' or 'rung of a ladder,' but it extends metaphorically to 'degree' or 'rank.' Paul uses it in 1 Timothy 3:13 to say that deacons who serve well 'gain a good standing (βαθμὸν καλόν) for themselves.' The term suggests upward mobility or advancement—faithful service earns a higher degree of honor or confidence. Classical usage includes steps, musical intervals, and degrees of rank. Paul's point is that diaconal ministry is not a dead-end role but a proving ground where faithfulness yields respect and perhaps positions one for further leadership.

senses.1: The translations (English 'standing,' Spanish 'posición,' German 'Stufe') reflect the metaphorical sense of rank or position. 1 Timothy 3:13 uses βαθμός to promise that deacons who serve well acquire a good 'standing'—an earned reputation or degree of influence that honors their proven character and opens doors for continued ministry impact.

gloss_terse: to dig deep, deepen, make deep; to excavate or hollow out
gloss_readable: This verb means 'to dig deep' or 'deepen,' describing the action of excavating to create depth. Jesus uses it in His parable of the two builders (Luke 6:48): the wise builder 'dug deep' (ἐβάθυνεν) and laid a foundation on rock, so when the flood came, the house stood firm. The term emphasizes the labor and foresight required to build on a solid base—it's not enough to build on the surface; one must dig down to bedrock. Classical usage includes deepening battle formations and hollowing out channels. Jesus' metaphor is transparent: hearing and obeying His words requires deep, costly commitment, not superficial assent.

senses.1: The evidence (English 'went deep,' Spanish 'profundizó,' French 'creuser profond') uniformly points to the action of digging deeply. Luke 6:48 uses ἐβάθυνεν to describe the wise builder's excavation work—he dug down through soil to reach rock, ensuring his foundation could withstand the storm. The verb captures the intentionality and effort required to obey Jesus' teaching thoroughly.

gloss_terse: palm branch, frond; the leafy branch of a palm tree, often used festively
gloss_readable: This noun denotes palm branches or fronds, the leafy boughs of palm trees. John describes the crowds welcoming Jesus into Jerusalem (John 12:13): they took 'palm branches' (βάϊα) and went out to meet Him, shouting 'Hosanna!' The gesture recalls the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israelites waved palm fronds in celebration, and evokes messianic expectation. Classical usage includes both palm branches and measuring rods. John's scene is loaded with irony: the crowd acclaims Jesus as king with symbols of victory and festival, unaware that His kingship will be realized not through military triumph but through crucifixion.

senses.1: The translations (English 'branches,' Spanish 'ramas,' French 'palme,' German 'Palmzweige') confirm the identification as palm fronds. John 12:13 uses βάϊα to describe the branches the crowd waved during Jesus' triumphal entry—a festive, nationalistic gesture that anticipated a conquering Messiah, even as Jesus rode toward the cross.

gloss_terse: Balak, the Moabite king; the ruler who hired Balaam to curse Israel
gloss_readable: This proper noun designates Balak, the Moabite king who hired the prophet Balaam to curse Israel during their wilderness journey (Numbers 22-24). In Revelation 2:14, Jesus rebukes the church at Pergamum for tolerating those who follow 'the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel.' The reference recalls Balaam's strategy of enticing Israel into idolatry and immorality when curses failed. Balak embodies the hostile Gentile ruler who seeks Israel's destruction through spiritual seduction rather than military force. Jesus' allusion warns that the ancient compromises are recycled in new forms within the church.

senses.1: The evidence simply transliterates the name (Balak, Balac) across languages, confirming its identity as the Moabite king. Revelation 2:14 invokes Balak to recall the Numbers narrative: he couldn't curse Israel directly, so he used Balaam to induce them to curse themselves through sin—a cautionary tale of compromise that Jesus applies to the Pergamene church's toleration of false teaching.

gloss_terse: Barak, the Israelite judge; the military leader who defeated Sisera under Deborah's guidance
gloss_readable: This proper noun designates Barak, the Israelite military commander who, at the prophetess Deborah's urging, led the army against the Canaanite general Sisera (Judges 4-5). In Hebrews 11:32, the author lists Barak among the heroes of faith who 'through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises.' Barak's inclusion is somewhat surprising given his initial reluctance to go without Deborah, yet he obeyed and achieved victory. The catalogue in Hebrews celebrates not moral perfection but faithful action—Barak trusted God's word through Deborah and fought accordingly. His name evokes the era of the judges, when faith and obedience brought deliverance.

senses.1: The evidence simply transliterates the name (Barak) uniformly, identifying him as the Judges-era leader. Hebrews 11:32 includes Barak in the honor roll of faith, reminding readers that even hesitant obedience—he agreed to fight only if Deborah accompanied him—counts as faith when it yields to God's command and trusts His promise of victory.

gloss_terse: Barachiah, a personal name; father of the prophet Zechariah
gloss_readable: This proper noun designates Barachiah (Hebrew: 'Yahweh has blessed'), identified in Matthew 23:35 as the father of Zechariah, whom Jesus says was murdered 'between the sanctuary and the altar.' The reference is debated: it may allude to Zechariah son of Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 24), martyred in the temple court, or to the canonical prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah. Either way, Jesus invokes the murder of a righteous prophet to indict the scribes and Pharisees for continuing their ancestors' pattern of violence against God's messengers. Barachiah's mention anchors the martyrdom in Israel's historical memory.

senses.1: The evidence simply transliterates the name (Barachias, Barachie) across languages, confirming it as a patronymic. Matthew 23:35 uses Βαραχίου to identify Zechariah's father, situating the prophet's murder within the genealogical and historical record that Jesus cites to hold His contemporaries accountable for a legacy of rejecting and killing those sent by God.

gloss_terse: Bar-Jesus, a personal name; the Jewish sorcerer also called Elymas
gloss_readable: This proper noun designates Bar-Jesus (Aramaic: 'son of Joshua'), the Jewish false prophet and sorcerer whom Paul encountered on Cyprus (Acts 13:6-12). Also called Elymas, he opposed Paul and Barnabas, trying to turn the proconsul away from the faith. Paul, filled with the Spirit, struck him with temporary blindness—a sign-judgment that led to the proconsul's conversion. The name 'son of Jesus/Joshua' is deeply ironic: this 'son of the Savior' is actually a child of the devil (Acts 13:10), a faker who perverts the gospel. Luke's account underscores the spiritual battle between true and false prophets.

senses.1: The evidence simply transliterates the name (Bar-Iesous, Bar-Jésus) across languages, identifying him as the Cypriot magician. Acts 13:6 introduces Βαριησοῦ as a Jewish false prophet whose opposition to Paul triggers a dramatic confrontation—his blindness becomes an acted parable of his spiritual condition and a catalyst for the Roman official's faith.

gloss_terse: Bar-Jonah, a personal name; patronymic surname of Simon Peter, son of Jonah
gloss_readable: This proper noun designates Bar-Jonah (Aramaic: 'son of Jonah'), the patronymic surname of Simon Peter. Jesus addresses him with this name in Matthew 16:17: 'Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven.' The moment follows Peter's confession that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of the living God. By invoking Peter's full Aramaic name, Jesus personalizes the blessing and underscores the divine origin of Peter's insight—it was not human reasoning but heavenly revelation. Bar-Jonah roots Peter in his Jewish identity even as he receives a new identity as 'Rock.'

senses.1: The evidence simply transliterates the name (Bar-Iōna, Bar-Jonas) across languages, confirming it as Peter's patronymic. Matthew 16:17 uses Βαριωνᾶ to address Peter at the climactic moment of his confession—the Aramaic name emphasizes both Peter's human lineage and the supernatural source of his revelation, bridging his earthly identity and his heaven-bestowed calling.

gloss_terse: Bartimaeus, a personal name; the blind beggar healed by Jesus near Jericho
gloss_readable: This proper noun designates Bartimaeus (Aramaic: possibly 'son of Timaeus' or 'son of the unclean'), the blind beggar whom Jesus healed as He left Jericho (Mark 10:46-52). Mark uniquely provides the man's name and patronymic, suggesting he became known in the early Christian community. Bartimaeus's persistent cries—'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!'—overcome the crowd's attempts to silence him, and Jesus commends his faith: 'Go; your faith has made you well.' The healed man immediately follows Jesus on the road—a picture of discipleship born from divine mercy and personal persistence.

senses.1: The evidence simply transliterates the name (Bartimaios, Bartimée, Bartimaeos) across languages, identifying him as the Markan blind beggar. Mark 10:46 introduces Βαρτιμαῖος with unusual specificity (including his father's name), perhaps because he became a recognizable disciple in the Jerusalem church—his healing and subsequent following of Jesus model the journey from spiritual blindness to sight and discipleship.

gloss_terse: very costly, extremely expensive; of great value or price
gloss_readable: This adjective means 'very costly' or 'extremely expensive,' describing something of exceptional value. Matthew uses it to describe the alabaster flask of 'very expensive ointment' (μύρου βαρυτίμου) that a woman poured on Jesus' head at Bethany (Matt 26:7). The disciples objected to the 'waste,' calculating the ointment's market value, but Jesus defended her act as a beautiful preparation for His burial. The term underscores the extravagance of her devotion—she gave what was most precious, and Jesus honored her gift as prophetic worship. Classical usage includes 'punishing severely,' but the New Testament sense is monetary and metaphorical value.

senses.1: The translations (English 'very expensive,' Spanish 'muy costoso,' French 'très précieux') emphasize high cost and value. Matthew 26:7 uses βαρυτίμου to describe the ointment's extraordinary worth—its expense measures the woman's devotion and sets up Jesus' rebuke of the disciples' utilitarian calculation, affirming that love's extravagance surpasses economic logic.

gloss_terse: torturer, jailer, one who examines by torture; an official who inflicts pain to extract confession or punish
gloss_readable: This noun denotes a torturer or jailer, one who examines prisoners through physical pain or administers judicial punishment. Jesus uses it in the parable of the unforgiving servant (Matt 18:34): the master, enraged by the servant's refusal to forgive, handed him over 'to the torturers' (τοῖς βασανισταῖς) until he should pay all his debt. The term evokes the brutal reality of ancient prison conditions and torture chambers. Jesus' point is chilling: unforgiveness imprisons the unforgiving in a hell of their own making. The βασανισταί symbolize the tormenting consequences of harboring grudges when one has received infinite mercy.

senses.1: The translations (English 'torturers,' Spanish 'verdugos,' French 'tortionnaire') uniformly point to those who inflict torture. Matthew 18:34 uses βασανισταῖς to depict the severe consequence of the unforgiving servant's hardness: he is delivered to torturers—a stark image of the spiritual and relational anguish that unforgiveness brings upon oneself, mirroring the judgment one refuses to extend as mercy.

gloss_terse: foot, base, stepping; the part of the body used for walking or standing
gloss_readable: This noun means 'foot' or 'base,' referring to the part of the body used for stepping or standing. Luke uses it in Acts 3:7 to describe the healing of the lame beggar: 'immediately his feet and ankles (βάσεις καὶ σφυδρά) were made strong.' The term emphasizes the structural foundation of locomotion—the βάσεις are not just anatomical feet but the literal bases that support standing and walking. Classical usage includes steps, rhythmic movements, and architectural bases. Luke's medical precision highlights the completeness of the healing: the man who had never walked now leaps and praises God, his βάσεις transformed from useless appendages to instruments of worship.

senses.1: The translations (English 'feet,' Spanish 'bases,' French 'base') confirm the anatomical sense. Acts 3:7 uses βάσεις to describe the lame man's feet, which were strengthened and enabled to bear weight—a miracle that symbolizes the gospel's power to restore what is broken and enable true worship.

gloss_terse: to bewitch, cast a spell on; to fascinate or enchant, often with malicious intent
gloss_readable: This verb means 'to bewitch' or 'cast a spell,' describing the act of enchanting or mesmerizing someone, often maliciously (by the 'evil eye'). Paul uses it rhetorically in Galatians 3:1: 'You foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you (τίς ὑμᾶς ἐβάσκανεν)?' He's not suggesting literal sorcery but rather expressing astonishment that the Galatians, who clearly saw Christ crucified depicted before them, have been so thoroughly deceived by false teachers. The term captures the irrational, almost supernatural quality of their apostasy—as if they've been placed under a spell that blinds them to the gospel's clarity.

senses.1: The translations (English 'bewitched,' Spanish 'fascinó,' German 'bezaubern') all point to enchantment or spell-casting. Galatians 3:1 uses ἐβάσκανεν metaphorically to express Paul's incredulity: the Galatians have been so thoroughly deceived by legalism that it's as if they've been bewitched, their spiritual vision obscured by a malevolent influence that contradicts the plain gospel they once embraced.

gloss_terse: bath, a Hebrew liquid measure; a unit of volume used for liquids, approximately 8-9 gallons
gloss_readable: This noun denotes the bath, a Hebrew liquid measure roughly equivalent to 8-9 gallons or 30-40 liters. Jesus uses it in the parable of the dishonest manager (Luke 16:6), where a debtor owes 'a hundred baths of oil' and the manager tells him to change the bill to fifty. The term grounds the parable in the economic realities of first-century Palestine, where large agricultural debts were calculated in standard measures. The manager's shrewd reduction of the debt (by half!) is scandalous yet commended by Jesus for its strategic foresight. The βάτος is a concrete unit that measures both the debt and the grace extended.

senses.1: The translations (English 'measures,' Spanish 'batos,' French 'baths') confirm the identification as a standard liquid measure. Luke 16:6 uses βάτους to quantify the olive oil debt in Jesus' parable—100 baths is a substantial quantity, and the manager's bold rewriting of the contract to 50 baths demonstrates the kind of decisive, self-interested action Jesus urges His disciples to emulate (in righteousness) for eternal purposes.

gloss_terse: frog, the amphibian; the small leaping creature associated with water and marshes
gloss_readable: This noun denotes frogs, the amphibious creatures familiar from marshes and streams. John uses it in Revelation 16:13, where he sees 'three unclean spirits like frogs' coming from the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet. The imagery evokes the plague of frogs in Exodus, a divine judgment on Egypt. In Revelation, the frog-like demons gather the kings of the earth for the battle of Armageddon—a grotesque, plague-like mobilization of evil. Classical usage includes literal frogs and the fishing-frog (angler fish). John's apocalyptic βάτραχοι symbolize unclean, pestilential spirits that seduce the nations into final rebellion.

senses.1: The translations (English/Spanish 'frogs,' French 'grenouilles,' German 'Frösche') uniformly identify the creatures. Revelation 16:13 uses βάτραχοι to describe unclean spirits that summon the world to war against God—an echo of the Exodus plague that underscores the demonic, repulsive nature of the spiritual forces driving human rebellion in the last days.

gloss_terse: to babble, use vain repetitions; to repeat words mindlessly or stammer
gloss_readable: This rare verb means 'to babble' or 'use vain repetitions,' describing speech characterized by meaningless repetition or stammering. Jesus uses it in the Sermon on the Mount (Matt 6:7): 'When you pray, do not babble (μὴ βατταλογήσητε) like the Gentiles, for they think they will be heard for their many words.' The term critiques pagan prayer practices that rely on verbal volume or magical formulas rather than genuine communion with a Father who knows what His children need. Classical usage suggests stammering or saying the same thing over and over. Jesus calls for simplicity and sincerity, not ritualistic verbosity.

senses.1: The translations (English 'babble,' Spanish 'usen vanas repeticiones,' French 'balbutier') all capture the idea of empty repetition. Matthew 6:7 uses βατταλογήσητε to warn against the pagan assumption that prayer effectiveness depends on word count or formulaic recitation—true prayer is relational conversation with a loving Father, not a magical incantation aimed at a distant deity.

gloss_terse: detestable, abominable, loathsome; morally or ritually repugnant
gloss_readable: This adjective means 'detestable' or 'abominable,' describing what is morally or ritually loathsome. Paul uses it in Titus 1:16 to describe false teachers who 'profess to know God, but by their works they deny Him, being detestable (βδελυκτοὶ) and disobedient.' The term, common in Septuagint contexts of idolatry and impurity, conveys visceral repugnance. These teachers are not merely wrong but βδελυκτοί—their hypocrisy and moral corruption make them abhorrent to God. Classical usage is rare in this exact form, but the Septuagint employs it for abominations. Paul's condemnation is total: their lives contradict their lips, rendering them detestable despite their claims.

senses.1: The translations (English 'detestable,' Spanish 'abominables,' German 'abscheulich') all emphasize loathsomeness and moral repugnance. Titus 1:16 uses βδελυκτοὶ to characterize those whose conduct belies their confession—they are detestable because their deeds expose their profession as a lie, making them objects of divine abhorrence rather than approval.

gloss_terse: Belial or Beliar, a name for Satan; a designation for the devil as adversary and embodiment of evil
gloss_readable: This proper noun designates Belial (or Beliar), a name for Satan used in Jewish literature and the New Testament. Paul employs it in 2 Corinthians 6:15: 'What accord has Christ with Beliar? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?' The term (from Hebrew בְּלִיַּעַל, 'worthlessness') became personified as a demonic figure or Satan himself. Paul uses it to underscore the absolute incompatibility between Christ and the powers of darkness. There can be no partnership, no middle ground—the covenant people must separate from the realm of Beliar and walk in the light.

senses.1: The evidence simply transliterates the name (Beliar, Bélial) across languages, confirming its identity as a designation for Satan. 2 Corinthians 6:15 uses Βελιάρ to personify evil in antithesis to Christ, arguing that believers cannot maintain spiritual fellowship with darkness—Beliar's domain is utterly opposed to Christ's kingdom, demanding radical separation and holiness.

gloss_terse: better, more excellent, preferable; of superior quality or advantage
gloss_readable: This comparative adjective means 'better' or 'more excellent,' describing what is superior or more advantageous. Paul uses the adverbial form in 2 Timothy 1:18: 'May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that Day—and you well know (βέλτιον οἶδας) all the service he rendered at Ephesus.' The term conveys 'very well' or 'better than I can say'—Paul defers to Timothy's firsthand knowledge of Onesiphorus's ministry. Classical usage often appears in ethical contexts ('becoming better,' 'advancing'). Paul's usage is affectionate: Timothy knows better than anyone the extent of Onesiphorus's devoted service, which will be rewarded on the Day of Judgment.

senses.1: The translations (English 'very well,' Spanish 'mejor,' German 'besser') confirm the comparative sense. 2 Timothy 1:18 uses βέλτιον to indicate superior knowledge—Timothy knows 'better' (more fully, more intimately) than Paul the many services Onesiphorus rendered at Ephesus, making Timothy a firsthand witness to the man's faithfulness and deserving of eschatological mercy.

gloss_terse: Beroean, a resident of Berea; pertaining to the city of Berea in Macedonia
gloss_readable: This adjective designates someone from Berea, the Macedonian city where Paul and Silas found a synagogue 'more noble' than Thessalonica's, examining the Scriptures daily to verify apostolic teaching (Acts 17:10-11). In Acts 20:4, Luke mentions Sopater the Beroean (Βεροιαῖος) among Paul's traveling companions on the collection journey to Jerusalem. The term marks geographical origin and, by association, evokes the Bereans' exemplary Scripture-searching spirit. Sopater's inclusion among the delegates underscores the unity of the multi-ethnic churches contributing to the Jerusalem relief fund. His identity as a Βεροιαῖος recalls the noble receptivity of his home synagogue.

senses.1: The evidence (English 'Beroiaios,' Spanish 'bereense,' French 'Béréen') confirms the demonym for Berea. Acts 20:4 identifies Sopater as Βεροιαῖος, linking him to the city where the Jews 'received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily'—his presence among Paul's companions honors Berea's legacy of thoughtful faith and generous partnership in the gospel.

gloss_terse: Bethzatha or Bethesda, a pool in Jerusalem; the site of Jesus' healing of the paralytic
gloss_readable: This proper noun designates Bethzatha (or Bethesda), the pool in Jerusalem where Jesus healed the man who had been paralyzed for thirty-eight years (John 5:2). The name's derivation is uncertain—perhaps from Aramaic meaning 'house of mercy' or 'house of the portico.' Archaeological excavations have uncovered a double pool near the Sheep Gate matching John's description. The site was associated with healing, attracting the sick who waited for the troubling of the water. John's account emphasizes Jesus' sovereign initiative: He seeks out the invalid and heals him without the ritual waters, demonstrating that true restoration comes from the life-giving Word, not magical springs.

senses.1: The evidence simply transliterates the name (Bēthzatha, Bethesda) across languages, with textual variants reflecting manuscript uncertainty. John 5:2 uses Βηθζαθά (in the best manuscripts) to identify the pool where the paralyzed man waited—a place of futile hope transformed by Jesus' presence into a site of miraculous liberation and Sabbath controversy.
